title: Why Durga has many arms
hookLine: the second story begins: every god gives the goddess something of his own, and the mountain gives her a lion
carry: every god's power, held by one goddess
tomorrow: The demon who keeps changing shape

lines: A TRIDENT, A DISCUS, A CONCH.
A CUP, A SNAKE, A LION.
cards: A trident. A discus. A conch.
A spear. A bow and two quivers of arrows. A thunderbolt, and a bell from an elephant's neck.
A staff. A noose. Prayer beads and a water pot.
A sword and a shield. An axe. Jewels, and a garland that never fades.

teach.h: EACH GIFT FROM THE GIVER'S OWN.
teach.b: In the second chapter the gods line up to give, and each gift comes out of the giver's own thing. Shiva draws a trident from his trident. Vishnu brings a discus out of his discus.
Varuna gives a conch and a noose. Agni, fire, gives a spear. Indra gives a thunderbolt from his own, and a bell from his elephant.
Brahma gives prayer beads and a water pot. The sun fills the pores of her skin with his rays. Kubera, lord of wealth, gives a full drinking cup.
And Himavat, the Himalaya itself, gives her a lion to ride. Notice the first gifts. Shiva, Vishnu and Indra don't hand over a spare; each draws a copy from his own power.
She carries all of it at once.
That's why the goddess Hindus know as Durga is shown with many arms, each hand holding a god's gift, riding a lion: for devotees she is the gods' combined power in one form.

Then she laughs, long and loud, and the sky fills with the sound. The earth shakes, and the demons rush toward the noise and see her, filling the three worlds with light. Mahisha's generals come at her with armies.
As she fights, the breaths she lets out become troops, beating drums and blowing conches.

teach.h: SHE CARRIES ALL OF IT AT ONCE.
teach.b: She breathes, and allies appear. Her lion stalks through the enemy, and the chapter ends with the armies in ruins, and Mahisha still to come.

how: Images of Durga in temples and in festival pandals during Navaratri and Durga Puja can show her many arms holding the weapons the gods gave her, riding a lion, as told in the Devi Mahatmya's second chapter.

games.q: you're at a Durga image with a friend who asks why she holds a trident and a discus. what do you say?
o: she collects weapons from every battle she wins.
Shiva and Vishnu gave them, each drawn from his own.
she made them herself, to show she needs no one.
games.why: the gods arm her from their own powers: Shiva a trident from his trident, Vishnu a discus from his discus. the mountain gives a lion.

practice: Find an image of Durga, in a home shrine, on your phone, or in your mind. Look at it slowly, hand by hand: the trident, Shiva's; the discus, Vishnu's; the conch, Varuna's; and under her, the mountain's lion.
Then take her in whole, all of it at once. Hindus call this darshan: seeing the deity, and, many say, being seen. If you pray, greet her in your own words; if you don't, simply look.

wordCard.voice: The Devi Mahatmya. Today, its second story: a goddess armed with each god's own gift, riding the mountain's lion, whose breaths become armies.

orig.note: Sanskrit: siṃha, lion. In the Devi Mahatmya, Himavat, the mountain, gives the goddess her lion.

carryVoice: Your line: every god's power, held by one goddess. Each gave from his own. That's today, done.
